title: Portable Inference Field Kit — Hands-on Playbook
content:
Overview:

This playbook is a compact, hands-on guide for running a short customer POC or workshop where the goal is to demonstrate a portable, low-latency inference setup that can be run on a small on-prem or edge cluster. It is intentionally pragmatic: minimal infra, reproducible steps, and a tiny shim to show routing/fallback behavior.

Primary objectives:
- Show customers a repeatable path to run the Redwood inference runtime in a constrained environment (single node k8s or an isolated VM).
- Demonstrate basic performance tuning knobs (batching window, kv-cache warmup, quantized model) and the observable impact.
- Walk through a simple canary/fallback: local -> dedicated hosted model fallback when local capacity is saturated.

Expected outcomes for participants:
- Deploy a local inference pod (container) with a quantized open model and the Redwood runtime image.
- Run a set of synthetic prompts and observe latency/throughput changes when toggling batching and cache settings.
- Exercise a fallback policy to a hosted Redwood model and validate request tracing.

Duration and target audience:
- 90 minutes workshop (40m setup/demo + 35m hands-on exercises + 15m wrap-up)
- Audience: platform engineers, solutions engineering POCs, technical product managers

Prerequisites (what we ask the customer to provide ahead of time):
- One small VM or single-node k8s cluster (4 vCPU, 16GB RAM recommended, GPU optional but preferred for throughput demos)
- Access to a private network or firewall rules to reach Redwood hosted control plane for optional fallback (or we can demo locally only)
- Docker and kubectl installed on the instructor laptop

Materials to bring:
- USB drive or shared GitHub repo with the portable-field-kit code and manifests
- Small sample dataset of prompts (included in repo)

Repo layout (what we use in the workshop):
- manifests/ : k8s pod/deployment and service manifests for a single-node demo
- docker/ : Dockerfile for a minimal runtime image (based on redwood/runtime:edge-preview)
- shim/ : small python routing shim (Flask) that shows local->hosted fallback and tracing headers
- scripts/ : helper scripts for generating load and measuring p95/p50 latency

Quick architecture summary (what we deploy) :
1) inference-pod: container running the Redwood-compatible runtime + quantized model (7B-quantized example)
2) routing-shim: a lightweight process in front of the inference process that implements a simple fallback policy
3) metrics-exporter: Prometheus-compatible endpoint that exposes per-request latency and token count

Step-by-step walkthrough (condensed)

1) Prepare the environment (10m)
- Clone repo: git clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/portable-field-kit.git
- Edit manifests/deployment.yaml to set IMAGE_TAG to the provided runtime image and set MODEL_URI to the quantized model tarball (example: s3://public-quant-models/7b-q4v2.tar)

2) Build & load image (if offline) (10m)
- If customer cannot pull from Docker Hub, build locally and load into the node: docker build -t redwood/portable-runtime:local -f docker/Dockerfile .
- kubectl apply -f manifests/namespace.yaml

3) Deploy inference pod (10m)
- Apply manifests: kubectl apply -f manifests/inference-deployment.yaml
- Verify: kubectl get pods -n portable-field-kit --> wait until inference-pod shows READY

4) Deploy routing shim and port-forward (5m)
- kubectl apply -f manifests/routing-shim-deployment.yaml
- Port-forward locally: kubectl port-forward svc/routing-shim 8080:80 -n portable-field-kit
- The shim exposes a /v1/generate endpoint that forwards to the local runtime or to hosted fallback based on simple rules (load or explicit header)

5) Run a quick smoke test (5m)
- curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"Hello from Redwood edge demo","max_tokens":32}'
- Expect JSON with tokens, latency_ms, and a tracing header redwood-trace-id

Sample routing-shim behavior (explain, pseudocode):
- On request: check local queue length and recent p95. If queue length > 5 or p95 > 1200ms, forward to hosted endpoint (fallback). Otherwise, forward to local runtime.
- Always attach trace header and a small synthetic call-id.

Minimal sample code (python shim excerpt):
# NOTE: this is a short illustrative snippet; full code in shim/ directory
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import requests
app = Flask(__name__)
LOCAL = 'http://inference-service:8081/v1/generate'
HOSTED = 'https://api.redwood.ai/v1/deployments/hosted-demo/generate'

@app.route('/v1/generate', methods=['POST'])
def gen():
    payload = request.get_json()
    # basic local health check metric (in practice use /metrics or health endpoint)
    local_ok = True  # replace with real check
    if local_ok:
        r = requests.post(LOCAL, json=payload, timeout=5)
    else:
        r = requests.post(HOSTED, json=payload, headers={'Authorization':'Bearer <TOKEN>'}, timeout=10)
    return jsonify(r.json())

Exercises (hands-on)
- Exercise A: Toggle batching window (batch_ms) from 20ms -> 100ms, run load generator (scripts/loadgen.py) at 10 qps and observe token cost vs latency. Note: larger batch_ms improves throughput but increases p95 for single requests.
- Exercise B: Warm KV cache using a set of prefix prompts and compare cold vs warm latency (present expected numbers for 7B-quantized vs unquantized).
- Exercise C: Trigger fallback by artificially limiting CPU on the inference pod (kubectl scale deployment --replicas=0) and observe that the shim routes to hosted and traces the latency.

Observability checklist (what to show)
- Prometheus metrics: request_latency_seconds_bucket, tokens_generated_total, fallback_count_total
- Logs: show trace id across shim and runtime logs (grep redwood-trace-id)
- Console: if customer has Redwood Console access, show a per-route latency/cost breakdown for fallback requests

Troubleshooting notes (common issues)
- Pod OOMs after model load: decrease model size or enable CPU-only quantized build; for GPU nodes, ensure NVIDIA drivers and device plugin are installed.
- High p95 and low throughput: confirm batching window and batching_max_tokens are configured as expected; check affinity/taints if node is throttled.
- Fallbacks not observed: validate the shim has network egress to hosted API and the API key is set in a secret.

Open questions / TODOs (for follow-up with customer)
- Should we include a small pre-warmed cache artifact to avoid cold start during demos? (Pros/cons: faster demo vs unrealistic expectation)
- Provide an optional exercise for local quantization using our recommend script: scripts/quantize_model.sh (requires GPU and time)
- Add a short section that compares running on a small GPU VM vs CPU-only node for common prompt types

Appendix: useful commands and snippets
- kubectl logs -n portable-field-kit -l app=inference -c runtime --tail=200\- kubectl port-forward svc/routing-shim 8080:80 -n portable-field-kit
- scripts/loadgen.py --target http://localhost:8080/v1/generate --qps 10 --duration 60
- quick curl example: curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8080/v1/generate -d '{"prompt":"short bullet list of benefits","max_tokens":48}' | jq

Notes to self (instructor tips):
- Start with an explicit cold start demo: show first request cold latency, then run a warmed request to highlight cache benefit.
- Keep fallback demo short and binary (either routes to hosted or not) to avoid network flakiness during customer sessions.
- Bring a pre-configured VM image in case cluster access is slow for participants.

End of playbook. Full manifests, shim code, and helper scripts are in the linked repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/portable-field-kit
